Water Quality Classification (2012-2024)¶

Final Project — Machine Learning

This notebook presents the exploratory analysis and AI prediction of the groundwater quality monitoring dataset from Mexico, published by CONAGUA and covering the period 2012–2024. The EDA aims to:

  • Understand the structure, coverage, and quality of the data.
  • Identify the behavior of physicochemical and microbiological parameters.
  • Justify the preprocessing decisions applied prior to modeling.
  • Explore the target variable (SEMÁFORO) and its relationship with the predictors.

This analysis logically precedes the predictive modeling stage (Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, and SVM) documented in the complementary notebook.

1. Load and Structure of the Dataset¶

The file contains three sheets: the main sheet CASUB_12-2024 with the monitoring data, a data dictionary sheet, and a sheet with classification scales by parameter. We worked exclusively with the main sheet.

1.1 Features Description & Target Description¶

The dataset includes variables of three types:

Type Variables
Georeferencing CLAVE SITIO, SITIO, ORGANISMO_DE_CUENCA, ESTADO, MUNICIPIO, ACUIFERO, SUBTIPO, LONGITUD, LATITUD
Physicochemical and microbiological parameters (numerical) Alkalinity, Conductivity, TDS, Fluorides, Hardness, Fecal Coliforms, Nitrates, Arsenic, Cadmium, Chromium, Mercury, Lead, Manganese, Iron
Classification variables CALIDAD_* (one per parameter), SEMÁFORO, CONTAMINANTES

The target variable for modeling is SEMÁFORO, which integrates all indicators into a three-level classification: GREEN (good water quality), YELLOW (intermediate quality), and RED (contaminated or unsafe water).

2. Data Quality¶

Before analyzing the numerical variables, it is necessary to quantify two issues affecting this dataset:

  1. Missing values (NaN): Some sites lack measurements for certain parameters, especially heavy metals, and the total amount of null in the numerical values is a total of 4450, the feature that has the most amount of null values is CR_TOT_mg/L between the chemical features.
  2. Censored values: Measurements reported as <X (below the instrument's detection limit). These are not null values, it is known that the contaminant is present, but its concentration is below a certain threshold.

Observations on Data Quality¶

  • Basic parameters (alkalinity, conductivity, TDS, hardness) have less than 5% missing values — they are the most reliable for modeling.
  • Fecal coliforms have ~18% missing values, which limits their usefulness as a predictor.
  • Heavy metals (Cd, Cr, Hg, Pb) show between 18% and 21% missing data, along with an additional proportion of values below the detection limit.
  • Imputation decision: Missing values are imputed using the mean of each variable. For censored values (<X), a value of 0 is assigned, which is a conservative convention assuming the lowest possible concentration.

3. Cleaning and Preparation for Numerical Analysis¶

We converted the numerical columns that were stored as text, handling the censored values.

In [ ]:
# Function to clean values
def clean_numeric(val):
    if pd.isna(val):
        return np.nan
    val = str(val).strip()
    if val.startswith('<'):
        return 0
    try:
        return float(val)
    except ValueError:
        return np.nan

# Apply to all features
for col in features:
    df[col] = df[col].apply(clean_numeric).astype(float)  # force float

# Fill missing values with column means
for col in features:
    df[col] = df[col].fillna(df[col].mean())

# Quick check
print("Missing values after cleaning:", df[features].isna().sum().sum())
print(df[features].dtypes)

import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
# Correct columns to be plotted
cols_to_plot = [col for col in df.columns if col != 'SEMÁFORO' and col != 'CONTAMINANTES' and col != 'ESTADO']

fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=7, ncols=2, figsize=(15, 20))
axes = axes.flatten()

for idx, col in enumerate(cols_to_plot):
    data = df[col].dropna()

    # Detect log_scale
    rango = data.max() / (data.min() + 1e-9) if data.min() >= 0 else None
    usar_log = rango is not None and rango > 100

    vals = np.log1p(data) if usar_log else data
    color = '#3498db' if usar_log else '#2ecc71'

    sns.histplot(data=vals, bins=30, color=color, edgecolor='white', ax=axes[idx], kde=False)

    titulo = f'{col}\n(escala log)' if usar_log else col
    axes[idx].set_title(titulo, fontweight='bold')

    # Median line
    median_val = np.log1p(data.median()) if usar_log else data.median()
    axes[idx].axvline(median_val, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, alpha=0.7)

    axes[idx].grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

# Hide empty subplots
for j in range(idx + 1, len(axes)):
    axes[j].set_visible(False)

# Legend
patch_log = mpatches.Patch(color='#3498db', label='Escala log (rango amplio)')
patch_lin = mpatches.Patch(color='#2ecc71', label='Escala lineal')
plt.legend(handles=[patch_log, patch_lin], loc='upper right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5. Features vs. Target: Which parameters distinguish water quality?¶

Boxplots by traffic-light category are the most relevant visualization for modeling: they allow us to visually see which variables have the greatest discriminative power among the three classes. If a variable shows no difference between GREEN, YELLOW, and RED, it will likely contribute little to the model.

In [ ]:
# Settings
cols_to_plot = [col for col in df.columns if col != 'SEMÁFORO' and col != 'CONTAMINANTES' and col != 'ESTADO']
ORDEN_SEMAFORO = ['VERDE', 'AMARILLO', 'ROJO']
COLORS_SEMAFORO = {'VERDE': '#2ecc71', 'AMARILLO': '#f1c40f', 'ROJO': '#e74c3c'}
colores_box = [COLORS_SEMAFORO[c] for c in ORDEN_SEMAFORO]

# Readable names
NOMBRES_LEGIBLES = {col: col for col in cols_to_plot}

# Create subplots
n_cols = 2
n_rows = math.ceil(len(cols_to_plot) / n_cols)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(15, n_rows*3))
axes = axes.flatten()

# Loop through columns
for i, col in enumerate(cols_to_plot):
    data_plot = df[[col, 'SEMÁFORO']].dropna()

    # Get data per group
    grupos = [data_plot[data_plot['SEMÁFORO'] == s][col].values for s in ORDEN_SEMAFORO]

    # Create boxplot manually
    bp = axes[i].boxplot(
        grupos,
        patch_artist=True,
        tick_labels=ORDEN_SEMAFORO,
        showfliers=False,
        medianprops=dict(color='black', linewidth=1.5)
    )

    # Set box colors
    for patch, color in zip(bp['boxes'], colores_box):
        patch.set_facecolor(color)
        patch.set_alpha(0.75)

    # Axes formatting
    axes[i].set_title(NOMBRES_LEGIBLES[col], fontsize=9)
    axes[i].tick_params(axis='x', labelsize=7)
    axes[i].tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=7)

    # Grids
    axes[i].grid(axis='both', linestyle='-', linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.7)

# Hide empty axes if any
for j in range(i + 1, len(axes)):
    axes[j].set_visible(False)

plt.suptitle(
    'Distribution of each variable by traffic-light category\n(without extreme outliers)',
    fontsize=13, y=1.02
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation of the Boxplots¶

The variables with the greatest visual separation among the three categories (highest discriminative power) are the ones that contribute most to the classification models. We observed:

  • Conductivity, TDS, and Alkalinity: Tend to be higher in RED sites, reflecting greater mineralization or diffuse contamination.
  • Fluorides: A critical variable in Mexico, elevated concentrations are an important indicator of natural contamination in aquifers.
  • Nitrates: Indicator of agricultural or wastewater contamination. Higher values are expected in RED sites.
  • Heavy metals (Arsenic, Cadmium, Chromium, Mercury, Lead): High concentration of zeros due to censored values; their discriminative power may be limited by the number of measurements below the detection limit.

7. Correlation Between Variables¶

We identified which pairs of variables measure related phenomena. A high correlation between predictors (multicollinearity) is especially relevant for Logistic Regression, which assumes a certain level of independence among input variables.

In [ ]:
# Get columns excluding 'SEMÁFORO'
cols_to_plot = [col for col in df.columns if col != 'SEMÁFORO' and col != 'CONTAMINANTES' and col != 'ESTADO']

# Calculate correlation matrix
corr_matrix = df[cols_to_plot].corr()

# Create mask for upper triangle (optional, remove if you don't want it)
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr_matrix, dtype=bool), k=1)

# Create the heatmap
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 10))
sns.heatmap(
    corr_matrix,
    mask=mask,
    cmap='RdYlGn',
    center=0,
    vmin=-1, vmax=1,
    annot=True, fmt='.2f',
    linewidths=0.5,
    square=True,
    ax=ax,
    annot_kws={'size': 8}
)

plt.title('Correlation Matrix of Physicochemical Features', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

8. Most Frequent Contaminants in RED Sites¶

The CONTAMINANTES column explicitly records which parameters exceed the standards in sites classified as RED. Analyzing their frequency tells us which water quality issues are most prevalent in Mexico according to this dataset.

In [ ]:
# Group data by state and traffic-light category,
# count occurrences, and pivot into a table format
estado_sem = df.groupby(['ESTADO', 'SEMÁFORO']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)

# Ensure all traffic-light categories exist as columns,
# even if some are missing in the dataset
for col in ORDEN_SEMAFORO:
    if col not in estado_sem.columns:
        estado_sem[col] = 0

# Reorder columns according to the desired traffic-light order
estado_sem = estado_sem[ORDEN_SEMAFORO]

# Compute total monitoring sites per state
estado_sem['TOTAL'] = estado_sem.sum(axis=1)

# Sort states from lowest to highest total
estado_sem = estado_sem.sort_values('TOTAL', ascending=True)

# Create figure and axis
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 9))

# Plot horizontal stacked bar chart
estado_sem[ORDEN_SEMAFORO].plot(
    kind='barh', stacked=True, ax=ax,
    color=[COLORS_SEMAFORO[c] for c in ORDEN_SEMAFORO],  # color per category
    edgecolor='white', linewidth=0.3  # subtle borders between segments
)

# Add total labels at the end of each bar
for i, (idx, row) in enumerate(estado_sem.iterrows()):
    ax.text(row['TOTAL'] + 2, i, f"{int(row['TOTAL'])}", va='center', fontsize=7.5)

# Axis labels and title
ax.set_xlabel('Number of monitoring sites')
ax.set_title('Distribution of monitoring sites by state and quality')

# Legend configuration
ax.legend(title='Traffic Light', loc='lower right')

# Adjust x-axis limit to leave space for labels
ax.set_xlim(0, estado_sem['TOTAL'].max() * 1.12)

# Improve layout to avoid overlaps
plt.tight_layout()

# Display plot
plt.show()

11. Predictive Models¶

The following blocks revisits the dataset incorporating predictive models:

  1. Class imbalance — class_weight='balanced' is added to all three models so that training penalizes errors in the minority class (YELLOW, 16.8% of the dataset) proportionally, without altering the data.
  2. Metrics — The classification_report (which already reports F1-score per class) is shown, and a row normalized confusion matrix is added to visualize per-class accuracy independently of class size.

Model: Decision Tree¶

We train a Decision Tree classifier with max_depth=6 to keep the model interpretable and avoid overfitting to the training data.

In [ ]:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# Define the model: Decision Tree
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=6,             # Maximum depth of the tree: limits how many splits are made (controls overfitting; deeper = more complex)
                              random_state=42,         # Seed for reproducibility (ensures same splits across runs)
                              class_weight='balanced') # Adjusts weights inversely proportional to class frequencies (helps with imbalanced datasets)

# Train the model
tree.fit(X_train, y_train)
Out[ ]:
DecisionTreeClassifier(class_weight='balanced', max_depth=6, random_state=42)

Evaluation¶

We evaluate the model on both the training and test sets. A small gap between the two accuracy scores indicates the model generalizes well without overfitting.

In [ ]:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Training predictions
y_train_pred = tree.predict(X_train)

# Test predictions
y_pred = tree.predict(X_test)

print("Train accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_train, y_train_pred))
print("Test accuracy: ", accuracy_score(y_test,  y_pred))

Test accuracy:  0.9413919413919414

Supported Vector Machine¶

In [ ]:
from sklearn.svm import SVC

svm = SVC(
    C            = 1000,       # Regularization parameter: high value -> tries to classify all training points correctly (less margin, risk of overfitting)
    gamma        = 0.01,       # Kernel coefficient for RBF: controls how far the influence of a single point reaches (low = smoother decision boundary)
    kernel       = 'rbf',      # Radial Basis Function kernel: good for non-linear relationships
    class_weight = 'balanced', # Adjusts weights inversely proportional to class frequencies (helps with imbalanced datasets)
    random_state = 42,         # Seed for reproducibility
)

# Training model
svm.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
